title: Numerical Investigation of Storm Surge Effects on Denitrification in Nearshore Aquifers
content:
Abstract

Coastal aquifers are highly dynamic environments, sensitive to both regular hydrodynamic forcing and extreme events. Among these, storm surges can significantly alter subsurface flow by expanding the upper saline plume (USP), modifying residence times, and intensifying mixing between fresh groundwater and seawater. These hydrological shifts significantly affect nitrogen transformation, particularly denitrification. This study uses reactive transport modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics to examine how the combined effects of storm surges and tides influence nitrate fate in a homogeneous, unconfined nearshore aquifer. Simulations reveal that storm surge rapidly increases nitrate removal, and that enhanced removal persists even after the surge subsides due to long-lasting changes in redox conditions and solute transport pathways. Sensitivity analyses show increased surge height enhances dissolved organic carbon influx and promotes both lateral and vertical expansion of the denitrification zone, thereby increasing nitrate removal efficiency. Surge duration primarily governs the temporal overlap between reactive solutes and thus controls the persistence of denitrification. Aquifer hydraulic conductivity regulates solute residence time and post-storm stability, whereas beach slope modulates the geometry and spatial extent of the reaction zone, with milder slopes supporting greater mixing and higher overall removal efficiency. These findings highlight the importance of extreme coastal events and aquifer properties in regulating coastal nitrogen cycling and provide valuable insights for nutrient management under changing climate conditions.
